title: Shipped Last Lighthouse on Android with Codex and Godot — phone playtesting changed the design
author: No_Manager8348
selftext:
I’ve released Last Lighthouse, a portrait lighthouse-defense game, and wanted to share what the AI-assisted process actually looked like. I direct the design and playtesting; Codex helped implement the Godot/GDScript game, native integrations and regression checks, and generative tools helped produce artwork.

The workflow was iterative: describe a change, implement it, run checks, build an Android APK, then play on a real phone. The phone sessions drove changes that a passing automated test couldn’t settle. Aiming over the lighthouse obscured the action, so the control moved underneath it. Long waves became short numbered levels. Boost selection, pause countdowns and percentage-based health needed repeated UX passes.

The distinction I keep coming back to is that code can pass checks while the game still feels wrong. Enemy pacing and the first few minutes need people who haven’t already learned every interaction. AI helped get revisions into a build, but deciding whether a change felt better came from playing it.

The current public Android release is free with ads, including optional video rewards: [https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.brewedapps.lastlighthouse](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.brewedapps.lastlighthouse)

I’d appreciate feedback on the opening and touch controls. For others building with AI: what playtest habit has caught the most problems your automated checks missed? This is my own commercial game, published through Brewed Apps.
